title: LoReC: Rethinking Large Language Models for Graph Data Analysis
claim: Models progressively neglect structured input as generation proceeds and are overly sensitive to its scaling, while our enhancement fixes this and improves results.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; three analysis plots then a bar chart
description: A 2x2 grid of data plots with serif captions below each: (a) Graph Tokens, (b) Text Tokens, (c) Scaling, (d) Performance Comparison. Panels (a) and (b) are line charts of attention value against generated length (0–55). Each has two lines, layer 0-16 in tan and layer 16-32 in slate blue, with shaded variance bands. Graph attention falls from about 0.14 to near 0.01–0.05, while text attention rises from about 0.86 to about 0.95–0.99. Panel (c) plots accuracy against scaling ratio (0.5–4.0). The red text-scaling line collapses sharply away from 1.0, while the blue graph-scaling line stays flat at about 0.6. Panel (d) is a grouped bar chart of Accuracy and Macro-F1 for Qwen3-8b, GraphPrompter and LoReC, with LoReC highest in accuracy. The muted blue, tan and red palette keeps the eye on the declining and rising curves first.
caption: (a-b) Attention distribution change between graph and text tokens across decoding layers as generation length increases. (c) Model performance under different scaling ratios applied to graph and text features. (d) Performance comparison of three approaches on the Citeseer dataset: text-only LLM baseline (Qwen3-8b), GraphPrompter, and LoReC-enhanced GraphPrompter.
abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has fundamentally reshaped the way we interact with graphs, giving rise to a new paradigm called GraphLLM. As revealed in recent studies, graph learning can benefit from LLMs. However, we observe limited benefits when we directly utilize LLMs to make predictions for graph-related tasks within GraphLLM paradigm, which even yields suboptimal results compared to conventional GNN-based approaches. Through in-depth analysis, we find this failure can be attributed to LLMs' limited capability for processing graph data and their tendency to overlook graph information. To address this issue, we propose LoReC (Look, Remember, and Contrast), a novel plug-and-play method for GraphLLM paradigm, which enhances LLM's understanding of graph data through three stages: (1) Look: redistributing attention to graph; (2) Remember: re-injecting graph information into the Feed-Forward Network (FFN); (3) Contrast: rectifying the vanilla logits produced in the decoding process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoReC brings notable improvements over current GraphLLM methods and outperforms GNN-based approaches across diverse datasets. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Git-King-Zhan/LoReC.
